items.title: Don Smedley and Tom Stagg Interview, 1969-10-03
items.q: The interviewee mentions Chris Barber's band coming into existence around 1952/1953 and notes that Ken Collier later 'chose Chris Barber on his rumbum' (likely meaning band/lineup) in 1954, but the interviewee does not claim a personal relationship, collaboration, or direct interaction with Barber h

ctx.x: Tom Stagg of London, England, 3rd October 1969. Talking about jazz in England from the earliest recollection, I have is about 1949, at that time there were probably only two or three jazz bands, mainly based on the early dance bands of the period. The dance bands of that period were Billy Cotton and Harry Roy. The Savoy Havana Band and the Savoy Ophians, which played at the Savoy Hotel in London for a long period for many years, from the late 1920s, the British jazz bands originated from this type of music,…
May I interrupt? Would you come from... come from, uh... the, uh... perhaps... 1949, the, uh, Ken Collier, the Queen River? You come from there. Yeah.

items.title: Don Smedley and Tom Stagg Interview, 1969-10-03
items.q: The interviewee discusses Chris Barber's role in the Ken Collier band and their subsequent split, but does not mention any personal interaction or direct relationship with Barber himself.

ctx.x: May I interrupt? Would you come from... come from, uh... the, uh... perhaps... 1949, the, uh, Ken Collier, the Queen River? You come from there. Yeah.

Ken Collier came back from New Orleans in, in, in late 1953, and this altered really the whole aspect of traditional jazz in England. The first thing he did was to, to get together the finest of the traditional musicians of that time in the country, and, um, he chose Chris Barber on his rumbum. Before that, for a very short period, a fellow called Ed MacDonald, who came from the north of England. He used Chris Barber and Dizz Disley on guitar, and banjo at that time. And these were the finest musicians of, of…
Now may I ask you, from where is Barry Martin spring?
